overview.title: 📖 Overview: Valuations, Assessments, and Consecrated Animals
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 20a–20b
overview.hebrewSource: חוֹמֶר בָּעֲרָכִין מִבַּנְּדָרִים: הָאוֹמֵר ״עֶרְכִּי עָלַי״ וָמֵת — יִתְּנוּ הַיּוֹרְשִׁים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by resolving Rava's dilemmas from the end of the previous daf about whether a vow of assessment (damim) requires a fresh court appraisal each time it is repeated — settled by the mishna's ruling about a vower who dies before any assessment was made. A new mishna then draws the mirror-image stringency: valuations (arakhin), fixed by the Torah, bind even a dead vower's heirs, while assessments (damim) do not, since 'there is no monetary value for the dead.' The mishna and Gemara then work through vows on limbs, on 'half' of oneself phrased two different ways, and on the valuation or assessment of someone else entirely. The daf closes with a fresh mishna distinguishing 'this bull is a burnt-offering' from 'it is incumbent upon me to bring this bull,' and a related dispute about consecrating something that does not yet exist.

slides.title: 🧮 Resolving Rava's Chain of Dilemmas
slides.subtitle: Does 'my assessment is incumbent upon me,' repeated or pre-existing, need a fresh appraisal?

nodes.content: ❓ Rava's dilemmas: one assessment or two for a double vow? Does an outside appraisal (by ten, not for the Temple) count?
📜 Proof offered: the mishna rules that if one vows 'my assessment is incumbent upon me' and dies before being appraised, heirs pay nothing, 'for there is no value for the dead'

columns.label: Suggested proof
columns.content: If an outside appraisal counted, every person is worth at least 4 zuz — so heirs should always owe something

columns.label: Gemara's rejection
columns.content: An outside appraisal 'enters into' a real assessment; a bare 'damai alai' with no appraisal at all never entered an assessment — the cases are not equivalent

nodes.content: ✅ The dilemmas are not fully resolved by this mishna alone — but the Gemara draws out what the ruling does and doesn't prove

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Must an assessment be performed with explicit intent for Temple consecration, or does any appraisal by a valid court suffice?

slides.title: ⚰️ Mishna: Valuations Are Stronger Than Assessments
slides.subtitle: What happens if the vower dies before paying?
rows: The sum is fixed by the Torah according to age and sex — nothing is 'lacking'
There is no monetary value for the dead, and the exact sum still needed a court appraisal
'The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,' and both die
Once he stood in judgment, his property was liened; the appraisal of the other is a mere disclosure
'The assessment of so-and-so is incumbent upon me,' the vower dies
His own obligation was fixed against him in judgment while alive
Same vow, but the subject of the vow dies
No monetary value can be fixed for a dead person

callout.label: Key move:
callout.text: The Gemara reads every 'heirs must pay' clause as referring specifically to a case where the vower 'stood in judgment' before death — the court's ruling functions like a debt written in a document.

slides.title: 🦵 Vowing a Limb: 'Nothing' vs. 'The Whole Valuation'
slides.subtitle: Only items the soul depends on trigger a full-body valuation

boxes.title: Says Nothing
items: Rav Giddel/Rav: still owes the assessment (damim) of the limb, per Rabbi Meir — 'a person does not speak for naught'

boxes.title: Owes Full Valuation
items: Principle: דָּבָר שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה תְּלוּיָה בּוֹ — an item the soul depends on
Includes the leg 'from the knee and above,' since severing it there is fatal

callout.label: Source:
callout.text: Leviticus 27:2, 'a valuation of living people (nefashot),' teaches that only a vow on something life-dependent triggers the full valuation of the entire self.

slides.title: ➗ Half My Valuation vs. The Valuation of Half of Me
slides.subtitle: Word order changes the bill completely — and the same split applies to assessments

steps.content: 1️⃣ 'Half of my valuation is incumbent upon me' → pays exactly half his valuation
2️⃣ 'The valuation of half of me is incumbent upon me' → pays his entire valuation, since 'half of a person' is life-dependent
3️⃣ Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda: even 'half of my valuation' is punished with lashes and must pay the full valuation — a rabbinic decree lest it be confused with 'valuation of half of me'
4️⃣ The identical split applies to assessments (damim): 'half of my assessment' vs. 'the assessment of half of me,' derived by juxtaposing neder and erekh in the same verse

callout.label: Vessels compared:
callout.text: Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis dispute a parallel case — vowing half the valuation of a vessel. Rava and Abaye explain the Rabbis follow both Rabbi Meir (no wasted words, so a whole vessel's valuation becomes its assessment) and Rabbi Shimon (only a typical act of donation takes effect — donating a whole vessel is typical, half a vessel is not).

slides.title: 🐂 'This Bull Is a Burnt-Offering' vs. 'It Is Incumbent Upon Me'
slides.subtitle: New mishna: who bears the loss if the animal dies or the house collapses?

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: 'This bull is a burnt-offering' or 'this house is an offering' — if it dies or collapses, he is exempt from replacing it.

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: But 'it is incumbent upon me to bring this bull/house as an offering' — if it dies or collapses, he is obligated to pay its value.

lines.speaker: R' Ḥiyya bar Rav
lines.text: This distinction only holds when he adds 'the monetary value of.' If he just says 'this bull is incumbent upon me,' the word 'this' ties the vow to that specific animal — he isn't responsible if it dies.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: A baraita seems to say even without 'monetary value,' saying 'incumbent upon me' creates liability for death or theft!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Both clauses of that baraita in fact discuss 'monetary value' vows — one where the bull itself is consecrated for its value, one where the future sale proceeds are consecrated (following Rabbi Meir, who allows consecrating something not yet in existence).

callout.label: Side halakha:
callout.text: A related Tosefta teaches that a landlord whose rented house is struck with leprosy may tell the tenant 'that which is yours is before you' while it stands — but once a priest has it dismantled, the landlord must supply a replacement house.

summary.principle: Torah valuations (arakhin) are fixed sums that survive the vower's death and bind his heirs, while vows of assessment (damim) depend on an actual court appraisal and lapse if the vower or the assessed party dies first; parallel rules govern vows on a single limb, on 'half' of oneself, and on a specific animal or house.

flowSteps.content: 🧮 Rava's chain of dilemmas on repeated/pre-existing assessments
⚰️ Mishna: 'my valuation' binds heirs even after death; 'my assessment' does not, absent a prior appraisal

columns.content: 🦵 Limb valuations: 'nothing' unless life-dependent (head, liver) — then full valuation
➗ 'Half my valuation' = half; 'valuation of half of me' = the whole, since it's life-dependent

flowSteps.content: 🐂 'This bull is an offering' (no liability if it dies) vs. 'incumbent upon me' (liability follows) — turns on the word 'value'
🎓 Key Principle: precise wording — erekh vs. damim, 'this' vs. 'incumbent upon me,' 'half' placed before or after — changes the vower's legal obligation entirely

quiz.q: Why does the mishna rule that heirs must pay a deceased person's Torah valuation (erekh) but not his vow of assessment (damim)?
o: Because valuations are always smaller amounts
Because the valuation is a fixed sum set by the Torah regardless of appraisal, while an assessment requires an actual court appraisal that never happened, and there is no monetary value for the dead
Because assessments can only be paid by the vower himself, never by anyone else
Because valuations apply only to those who die before old age
quiz.e: A Torah valuation is a fixed Torah sum keyed to age and sex, so nothing is 'lacking' after death. An assessment needs a court to determine the actual sum, and a dead person has no assessable monetary value.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what must one give if he vows 'the valuation of my head' or 'the valuation of my liver'?
o: Nothing, since valuations apply only to whole persons
Only the assessed value of that organ
The valuation of his entire self, since these are items the soul depends on
Half of his standard valuation
quiz.e: The principle 'an item the soul depends on' (davar she-hanshama teluya bo) means vowing such a body part triggers the valuation of one's whole self, derived from 'a valuation of living people' (Leviticus 27:2).

quiz.q: What is the difference between vowing 'half of my valuation' and vowing 'the valuation of half of me'?
o: They are legally identical
'Half of my valuation' pays half the valuation; 'the valuation of half of me' pays the full valuation, since half a person is life-dependent
'The valuation of half of me' pays nothing at all
'Half of my valuation' requires bringing an offering instead of money
quiz.e: Word order changes the vow's target: 'half of my valuation' simply halves the sum, but 'the valuation of half of me' targets something the soul depends on (you cannot survive being cut in half), triggering the full valuation.

quiz.q: Per Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav, why is one who says 'this bull is incumbent upon me as a burnt-offering' (without 'monetary value') exempt from liability if the bull dies?
o: Because the bull was never actually consecrated
Because saying 'this' ties the vow to that specific animal, so he only meant to commit to bringing it, not to bear financial responsibility for its value
Because animals are never subject to vows of assessment
Because he can substitute any other animal
quiz.e: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav explains that specifying 'this bull' shows he meant only to bring that particular animal as an offering, not to accept ongoing financial liability, unlike a vow that explicitly mentions the bull's 'monetary value.'

quiz.q: What halakha does the Gemara cite about a rented house afflicted with tzara'at (leprosy)?
o: The tenant must immediately vacate with no compensation ever
While the house still stands, the landlord may say 'that which is yours is before you'; but once a priest has it dismantled, the landlord must provide a replacement house
The landlord is exempt from any obligation to the tenant at all times
The house must be sold to the Temple treasury
quiz.e: A cited Tosefta teaches that a leprous house's owner is not liable to the tenant as long as the structure stands, but once it is actually dismantled by priestly ruling, he must supply the tenant with another house.
